items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 10.2 Electrolysing molten lead(II) bromide

items.label: text
items.text: Nothing at all happens until the lead(Il) bromide melts. Then:

items.label: list_item
items.text: the bulb lights up, showing that electrons are flowing through it

items.label: list_item
items.text: there is bubbling around the electrode (the anode) connected to the positive terminal of the power source as brown bromine gas is given off

items.label: list_item
items.text: nothing seems to be happening at the electrode (the cathode) connected to the negative terminal of the power source, but afterwards metallic lead is found underneath it

items.label: list_item
items.text: when you stop heating and the lead(Il) bromide solidifies again, everything stops, there is no more bubbling and the bulb goes out.

items.label: text
items.text: Lead(ll) bromide is an ionic compound. The solid consists of a giant structure of lead(Il) ions (Pb²+) and bromide ions (Br) packed regularly in a crystal lattice. The ions are locked tightly in the lattice and aren't free to move. The solid lead(ll) bromide doesn't conduct electricity. As soon as the solid melts, the ions become free to move around.

items.label: text
items.text: As soon as you connect the power source in Figure 10.2, it pumps any mobile electrons away from the left-hand electrode towards the right-hand one. This means that there are extra electrons at the right-hand electrode, so it is negative. The left-hand electrode is positive because some of the electrons have been removed from it. The positive lead(Ill) ions in the molten lead(Il) bromide are attracted to the negative electrode, the cathode. When they get there, each lead(Il) ion picks up two electrons from the electrode and forms neutral lead atoms (Figure 10.4). These fall to the bottom of the container as molten lead. This can be represented by a half-equation.

items.label: formula
items.text: P b ^ { 2 + } + 2 e ^ { - } \rightarrow P b

items.label: text
items.text: The power source pumps new electrons along the wire to replace the electrons that have been removed from the cathode.

items.label: text
items.text: Bromide ions are attracted to the positive electrode, the anode (Figure 10.5). When they get to the positive electrode, the extra electron which makes the bromide ion negatively charged moves onto the electrode. This is because this electrode is short of electrons.

items.label: text
items.text: The loss of the extra electron converts each bromide ion into a bromine atom:

items.label: formula
items.text: B r ^ { - } \rightarrow B r + e ^ { - }
